blocks.content: Ever copied and pasted code from one file to another?
It feels like a shortcut. But the moment that logic needs to change, you have to find every single copy and update them all. Miss one, and you have a bug.
That is the problem the DRY Principle solves.
DRY means "Don't Repeat Yourself." Every piece of logic should exist in one place only. Not two, not three, just one.
When code lives in one place, you fix it once, update it once, and test it once. That is what makes code easy to maintain.
The rest of this chapter shows you how.
1. What Is the DRY Principle?
"Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system." The Pragmatic Programmer
The DRY principle says that each piece of knowledge should live in exactly one place. When you need it somewhere else, you reference that single source instead of creating another copy.
Notice the quote says "knowledge", not "code." This is an important distinction. DRY is not just about avoiding duplicate lines. It applies to:

["Business rules: If \"orders above $100 get free shipping\" is a rule, it should be defined once, not checked in the checkout, the cart, and the invoice with slightly different conditions.","Configuration: Database URLs, API keys, and timeout values should live in one config file, not scattered across multiple classes.","Data models: If a Product has a price and stock, that structure should be defined once, not redefined in every module that uses it.","Documentation: If your API describes a field as \"Unix timestamp format,\" that definition should come from one source, not be manually repeated across three different doc pages.","Tests: Shared setup logic like creating a test order or seeding a database should be extracted into helpers, not copy-pasted across every test file."]
items: Business rules: If "orders above $100 get free shipping" is a rule, it should be defined once, not checked in the checkout, the cart, and the invoice with slightly different conditions.
Configuration: Database URLs, API keys, and timeout values should live in one config file, not scattered across multiple classes.
Data models: If a Product has a price and stock, that structure should be defined once, not redefined in every module that uses it.
Documentation: If your API describes a field as "Unix timestamp format," that definition should come from one source, not be manually repeated across three different doc pages.
Tests: Shared setup logic like creating a test order or seeding a database should be extracted into helpers, not copy-pasted across every test file.

blocks.content: Whenever the same concept appears in more than one place, you create redundancy. And redundancy makes your system harder to change and easier to break.
2. The Rule of Three
Before you rush to extract every repeated piece of code into a shared utility, there is an important guideline to keep in mind: the Rule of Three.

The idea is simple. Wait until you see the same pattern three times before extracting it. Two occurrences might just be a coincidence. Those two pieces of code may look similar today but could evolve in completely different directions tomorrow as their features grow apart. Three occurrences, though, that is a pattern.
At that point, you have strong evidence that the duplication represents genuine shared knowledge, and pulling it into a single location is the right call.

Think of it like this. The first time you write something, you just write it. The second time you see something similar, you notice it but hold off. The third time, you stop and extract it. That rhythm keeps you from over-engineering early while still protecting you from the long-term pain of true repetition.
["Once: Just write it. No action needed.","Twice: Take note. It might be a coincidence.","Three times: Extract it. You have found real shared knowledge."]
items: Twice: Take note. It might be a coincidence.
Three times: Extract it. You have found real shared knowledge.

blocks.content: The Rule of Three is not about being lazy or sloppy. It is about being deliberate. Premature abstraction can be just as painful as duplication. Wait for the pattern to prove itself before you act on it.
Imagine you are building a library management system with three modules:registration, borrowing, and fines.Each module checks whether a member is old enough to register, which is 16 or above.

Now the library changes its policy. The minimum age is now 18. You have to go into every single module and update the number. Miss one, and a 17 year old can still borrow books but cannot register. Or they can register but cannot be charged a fine.
Three modules. Three copies. Three chances to make a mistake.
This is the real danger of duplication. It is not just extra typing. It is a system that can silently contradict itself. One part says yes, another says no, and nobody knows which one is right.
The fix is simple. Write the rule once, and let every module refer to that one place. Change it once, and the whole system stays consistent.
3. Why Repetition Is a Problem
Copying code feels harmless in the moment. But as your project grows, that decision quietly becomes a liability. Here is why.
1. One Change Becomes Many

When logic lives in multiple places, a single update turns into a treasure hunt. You have to track down every copy, remember where you pasted it, and hope you do not miss one. In a large codebase with many contributors, you will miss one. And that missed copy will cause a bug at the worst possible time.
2. Copies Drift Apart

Two pieces of code that look identical today will not stay that way. One developer improves one copy but forgets the other. Now you have two versions of the same rule behaving differently. Your system starts contradicting itself, and nobody knows which version is correct.
3. Reading Code Becomes Harder

When the same logic is scattered across dozens of files, it is difficult to tell what is unique and what is repeated. New developers waste time reading the same block over and over trying to figure out if there is a difference. There usually is not. It is just noise.
4. Testing the Same Thing Twice

Duplicated logic needs duplicated tests. Every copy needs its own test cases covering the same behavior. When the rule changes, every test file needs updating too. In reality, developers update one or two and move on. The rest quietly become outdated and give you false confidence.
Repetition does not just make code messy. It makes it untrustworthy.
4. Copy-Paste Is a Red Flag
The moment you paste code you already wrote somewhere else, stop and ask yourself one question:
If this logic changes, how many places will I have to update?
If the answer is more than one, you are not saving time. You are borrowing it. And you will pay it back later, with interest, in the form of bugs, confusion, and late night debugging sessions.
Copy-paste is not always wrong. But it is always a warning sign worth paying attention to.
5. Applying DRY
Let us go back to the library example and fix it properly.
Step 1: Create a Utility Class
Instead of repeating the age check everywhere, we pull it into one dedicated class.
Step 2: Use It Across Modules
Every module now calls this one class instead of checking the age on its own.

The age rule now lives in exactly one place. Tomorrow if the library decides to change the minimum age to 21, you update a single number in MemberEligibility and every module in the system reflects that change instantly.
One class. One rule. Zero confusion.

blocks.content: DRY is powerful, but blindly following it can actually make your code worse. Sometimes repetition is the right choice.
Premature Abstractions Do More Harm Than Good

blocks.content: Imagine you see the same phone check written twice and immediately extract it into a shared class. Two weeks later, one module needs to validate landlines differently from mobile numbers. Now your abstraction is wrong for both, and untangling it is harder than if you had just left the duplication alone.
Wait for the pattern to prove itself. Write it twice, observe it, then decide.
"Duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction." Sandi Metz
Similar Code Is Not Always the Same Knowledge
blocks.text: Similar Code Is Not Always the Same Knowledge

blocks.content: Two modules both check if a phone number is 10 digits. They look identical today. But one is checking member registration numbers and the other is checking emergency contact numbers. Same logic, completely different reasons.
If you merge these and the registration rule changes to 11 digits, you accidentally break emergency contacts too. Here repetition is not a problem. It is protection.
Some Things Are Too Simple to Abstract
blocks.text: Some Things Are Too Simple to Abstract

blocks.content: Not every repeated line deserves its own method. If two modules both write age >= 18, creating a whole utility class around it is not DRY. It is overengineering.
Extract logic that changes and matters.Leave alone logic that is simple and obvious.
7. Practical Example: Booking System

Let us look at a real scenario. You have three services, HotelService, FlightService, and CarService, that all send booking confirmations to users. Each service duplicates the same two things: building the message and delivering it.
The Problem: Before DRY

codes.python:
class HotelService:
    def confirm_booking(self, user_id, hotel_id):
        # Duplicated: building message
        message = f"[Hotel] Dear {user_id}, your hotel {hotel_id} is confirmed."
        formatted = message[0].upper() + message[1:]

        # Duplicated: delivering message
        print("Connecting to delivery API...")
        print(f"Sending to {user_id}: {formatted}")
        print("Message delivered.")


class FlightService:
    def confirm_booking(self, user_id, flight_id):
        # Duplicated: building message
        message = f"[Flight] Dear {user_id}, your flight {flight_id} is confirmed."
        formatted = message[0].upper() + message[1:]

        # Duplicated: delivering message
        print("Connecting to delivery API...")
        print(f"Sending to {user_id}: {formatted}")
        print("Message delivered.")


class CarService:
    def confirm_booking(self, user_id, car_id):
        # Duplicated: building message
        message = f"[Car] Dear {user_id}, your car {car_id} is confirmed."
        formatted = message[0].upper() + message[1:]

        # Duplicated: delivering message
        print("Connecting to delivery API...")
        print(f"Sending to {user_id}: {formatted}")
        print("Message delivered.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    HotelService().confirm_booking("Alice", "H-101")
    FlightService().confirm_booking("Alice", "F-202")
    CarService().confirm_booking("Alice", "C-303")

blocks.content: 8. Why This Works
One place for messages. Need to change the greeting from "Dear" to "Hello"? Update BookingMessageBuilder once and every service reflects it instantly.
One place for delivery. If the API changes or you need to add retry logic, you touch BookingNotifier only. Nothing else breaks.
Each service stays focused. HotelService only knows about hotels. It does not care how messages are built or delivered. That is not its job.
Easy to grow. Adding a TrainService tomorrow requires zero changes to existing code. Just call the same two classes and you are done.
